title: Martingales and Optimal Stopping
summary: A martingale is the mathematical model of a fair game: whatever has happened so far, the expected future fortune equals the present fortune. The concept is simple, but it is one of the most powerful tools in probability. It gives short solutions to…

intro.x: A martingale is the mathematical model of a fair game: whatever has happened so far, the expected future fortune equals the present fortune. The concept is simple, but it is one of the most powerful tools in probability. It gives short solutions to hitting-time problems (gambler’s ruin, waiting for patterns), sharp concentration inequalities, almost sure convergence theorems, and the theory of optimal stopping.

Throughout, $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are random variables describing the randomness revealed step by step, and $\F_n$ denotes “the information in $X_1,\dots,X_n$” (with $\F_0$ the trivial information). We write $\Exp[Y\given\F_n]$ for $\Exp[Y\given X_1,\dots,X_n]$, the conditional expectation given the vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$, defined as in Chapter 10. It satisfies the same properties: linearity, taking out what is known, independence, the tower property $\Exp[\Exp[Y\given\F_n]\given\F_m]=\Exp[Y\given\F_m]$ for $m\le n$, and the defining property $\Exp[g(X_1,\dots,X_n)Y]=\Exp[g(X_1,\dots,X_n)\Exp[Y\given\F_n]]$.

blocks.x: A sequence $(M_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a martingale if
$M_n$ is determined by $X_1,\dots,X_n$ (adapted),
$\Exp\abs{M_n}<\infty$, and
$\Exp[M_{n+1}\given\F_n]=M_n$ for all $n$.
It is a submartingale if $\Exp[M_{n+1}\given\F_n]\ge M_n$ (a favourable game) and a supermartingale if $\le$ (an unfavourable game).

Taking expectations (tower property), $\Exp[M_n]=\Exp[M_0]$ for a martingale, and by the tower property $\Exp[M_n\given\F_m]=M_m$ for all $m\le n$. The increments $D_n=M_n-M_{n-1}$ satisfy $\Exp[D_n\given\F_{n-1}]=0$.
Random walk. If the $X_i$ are independent with mean $\mu$ and $S_n=\sum_{i\le n}X_i$, then $S_n-n\mu$ is a martingale: $\Exp[S_{n+1}-(n+1)\mu\given\F_n]=S_n+\mu-(n+1)\mu$.
Squared walk. If $\Exp[X_i]=0$ and $\Var(X_i)=\sigma^2$, then $S_n^2-n\sigma^2$ is a martingale: $\Exp[S_{n+1}^2\given\F_n]=S_n^2+2S_n\Exp[X_{n+1}]+\sigma^2$.

Exponential martingale. If $M(\theta)=\Exp[e^{\theta X_i}]<\infty$, then $e^{\theta S_n}/M(\theta)^n$ is a martingale. For the biased simple walk ($\Prob(X=1)=p$), choosing $\theta=\ln(q/p)$ gives $M(\theta)=p\cdot\frac qp+q\cdot\frac pq=1$, so $(q/p)^{S_n}$ is a martingale.
Products. If $Y_i\ge0$ are independent with $\Exp[Y_i]=1$, then $\prod_{i\le n}Y_i$ is a martingale.
Doob martingale. For any integrable $Y$, $M_n=\Exp[Y\given\F_n]$ is a martingale (tower property). Learning information step by step, our estimate of $Y$ is a martingale.

P'olya’s urn. An urn has $r_0$ red and $b_0$ blue balls; at each step a ball is drawn, returned, and one extra ball of the same colour added. If $R_n$, $B_n$ are the numbers after $n$ steps, then the fraction $F_n=R_n/(R_n+B_n)$ is a martingale. Indeed $R_n+B_n=r_0+b_0+n=:T_n$ is deterministic, and

\Exp[R_{n+1}\given\F_n]=R_n+\frac{R_n}{T_n}=R_n\frac{T_n+1}{T_n},\quad\text{so}\quad
\Exp[F_{n+1}\given\F_n]=\frac{R_n(T_n+1)/T_n}{T_n+1}=F_n.
Branching process. If $Z_n$ is the generation size with mean offspring $m$, then $Z_n/m^n$ is a martingale.
You cannot beat a fair game
A process $(H_n)_{n\ge1}$ is predictable if $H_n$ is determined by $X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}$: the bet at time $n$ may use only the past.
If $M$ is a martingale and $H$ is predictable and bounded, then $(H\cdot M)_n=\sum_{k=1}^nH_k(M_k-M_{k-1})$ is a martingale, with $\Exp[(H\cdot M)_n]=0$.

$H_k$ is $\F_{k-1}$-measurable and bounded, so by “taking out what is known”, $\Exp[H_k(M_k-M_{k-1})\given\F_{k-1}]=H_k\Exp[M_k-M_{k-1}\given\F_{k-1}]=0$. Hence $\Exp[(H\cdot M)_{n+1}\given\F_n]=(H\cdot M)_n$.

Interpreted as betting: $H_k$ is the stake on round $k$ (decided in advance), $M_k-M_{k-1}$ is the gain per unit staked, and the total winnings are still a fair game. No predictable betting system can create an advantage.

sections.title: Stopping times and the optional stopping theorem

blocks.x: A random time $\tau\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ is a stopping time if for every $n$ the event $\{\tau=n\}$ is determined by $X_1,\dots,X_n$: the decision to stop at time $n$ uses only the information available at time $n$.
For example, “the first time the walk hits $10$” is a stopping time; “the last time before $100$ that the walk is at its maximum” is not (it needs the future).
If $M$ is a martingale and $\tau$ a stopping time with $\tau\le K$ for a constant $K$, then $\Exp[M_\tau]=\Exp[M_0]$.

Let $H_k=\indic_{\{\tau\ge k\}}=1-\indic_{\{\tau\le k-1\}}$, which is determined by $X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}$, so $H$ is predictable and bounded. Then $M_{\tau\wedge n}=M_0+\sum_{k=1}^nH_k(M_k-M_{k-1})=M_0+(H\cdot M)_n$, a martingale by Theorem 14.4, so $\Exp[M_{\tau\wedge n}]=\Exp[M_0]$ for all $n$. Take $n=K$.
Let $M$ be a martingale and $\tau$ a stopping time with $\tau<\infty$ almost surely. Then $\Exp[M_\tau]=\Exp[M_0]$ if any of the following holds:
$\tau$ is bounded;
$\abs{M_{\tau\wedge n}}\le K$ for all $n$ (the stopped process is bounded);
$\Exp[\tau]<\infty$ and the increments are bounded: $\abs{M_n-M_{n-1}}\le c$.

(a) is Theorem 14.6. In (b) and (c) we have $\Exp[M_{\tau\wedge n}]=\Exp[M_0]$ and $M_{\tau\wedge n}\to M_\tau$ almost surely (as $\tau<\infty$). In (b) the sequence is bounded, so the bounded convergence theorem gives $\Exp[M_{\tau\wedge n}]\to\Exp[M_\tau]$. In (c), $\abs{M_{\tau\wedge n}}\le\abs{M_0}+c\tau$, which is integrable, and dominated convergence applies.

Let $S_n$ be the symmetric simple random walk from $0$ and $\tau=\min\{n:S_n=1\}$. Then $\tau<\infty$ a.s. (recurrence), yet $S_\tau=1$ while $\Exp[S_0]=0$. The theorem fails because $\Exp[\tau]=\infty$ and $S_{\tau\wedge n}$ is unbounded below. The doubling strategy “bet $1$, double after every loss, stop at the first win” always ends with a profit of $1$, but only by risking unbounded losses along the way. Optional stopping formalises why there is no free lunch under a finite credit limit or a bounded time.
Applications

For the symmetric walk from $k$ with $\tau=\min\{n:S_n\in\{0,N\}\}$: $\tau<\infty$ a.s. and $\Exp[\tau]<\infty$, because from any state the walk exits within $N$ steps with probability at least $2^{-N}$, so $\Prob(\tau>mN)\le(1-2^{-N})^m$ and $\Exp[\tau]=\sum_n\Prob(\tau>n)<\infty$. The stopped walk is bounded by $N$, so Theorem 14.7(b) gives $k=\Exp[S_\tau]=N\cdot\Prob(S_\tau=N)$, i.e. $h_k=k/N$. For the duration, $(S_n-k)^2-n$ is a martingale (Example 14.2(2) applied to the increments), so $\Exp[(S_{\tau\wedge n}-k)^2]=\Exp[\tau\wedge n]$ for every $n$. Let $n\to\infty$: $\tau\wedge n\uparrow\tau$ (monotone convergence on the right) and $S_{\tau\wedge n}$ is bounded by $N$ (bounded convergence on the left), so
\Exp[\tau]=\Exp[(S_\tau-k)^2]=(N-k)^2\frac kN+k^2\Bigl(1-\frac kN\Bigr)=k(N-k),
confirming Theorem 12.4. For the biased walk use the martingale $(q/p)^{S_n}$: with $r=q/p$, $r^k=h\,r^N+(1-h)$, so $h=(1-r^k)/(1-r^N)$, again agreeing with Theorem 12.1.
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be i.i.d. with $\Exp\abs{X_1}<\infty$ and mean $\mu$, and let $\tau$ be a stopping time with $\Exp[\tau]<\infty$. Then
\Exp\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^\tau X_i\Bigr]=\mu\,\Exp[\tau].

By optional stopping for the bounded stopping time $\tau\wedge n$ applied to the martingale $S_k-k\mu$: $\Exp[S_{\tau\wedge n}]=\mu\Exp[\tau\wedge n]$. As $n\to\infty$, the right side tends to $\mu\Exp[\tau]$ by monotone convergence. For the left side, $S_{\tau\wedge n}\to S_\tau$ and $\abs{S_{\tau\wedge n}}\le\sum_{k=1}^\tau\abs{X_k}$, whose expectation is

\sum_{k\ge1}\Exp\bigl[\abs{X_k}\indic_{\{\tau\ge k\}}\bigr]=\sum_{k\ge1}\Exp\abs{X_1}\Prob(\tau\ge k)
=\Exp\abs{X_1}\Exp[\tau]<\infty,
since $\{\tau\ge k\}$ is determined by $X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}$ and so is independent of $X_k$. Dominated convergence finishes the proof.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Expected waiting time for a pattern

blocks.x: Toss a fair coin until a given pattern of length $m$ appears; let $\tau$ be the first time it does. Claim:
\Exp[\tau]=\sum_{k=1}^m2^k\,\indic\{\text{the first }k\text{ letters of the pattern equal its last }k\text{ letters}\}.

Proof. Before each toss $j$ a new gambler arrives with a fortune of $1$ rupee and bets it all on toss $j$ showing the first letter of the pattern. If he loses he is out; if he wins his fortune doubles to $2$ and he bets all of it on toss $j+1$ showing the second letter, and so on until the pattern is completed (every bet is fair). Let $M_n$ be the total fortune of all gamblers present up to time $n$ minus the total amount put in, $n$: it is a martingale (a sum of fair bets) with increments bounded by $2^m$, and $\Exp[\tau]<\infty$ (the pattern appears in each block of $m$ tosses with probability $2^{-m}$). By Theorem 14.7(c), $\Exp[M_\tau]=0$, i.e. $\Exp[\text{total fortune at }\tau]=\Exp[\tau]$.

At time $\tau$ the pattern has just been completed, so the gambler who started $m$ tosses earlier holds $2^m$. A gambler who started $k<m$ tosses earlier is still alive exactly when the last $k$ tosses equal the first $k$ letters of the pattern, in which case he holds $2^k$; all others hold $0$. The last $k$ tosses are the last $k$ letters of the pattern, so the condition is the overlap condition in the claim, and the total fortune is the stated sum. $\square$

Examples: HH $\to2^1+2^2=6$ (overlaps at $k=1$ and $k=2$); HT $\to2^2=4$ (only the full pattern overlaps; this matches Example 10.7); HHH $\to2+4+8=14$; HTH $\to2+8=10$; TTH $\to8$. For HHTHH the overlaps are at $k=1$ (H $=$ H), $k=2$ (HH $=$ HH) and $k=5$, giving $2+4+32=38$.
If $M$ is a non-negative submartingale, then for $\lambda>0$, $\Prob\bigl(\max_{k\le n}M_k\ge\lambda\bigr)\le\Exp[M_n]/\lambda$.

Let $A_k=\{M_k\ge\lambda,M_j<\lambda\ \text{for }j<k\}$, which is determined by $X_1,\dots,X_k$; the $A_k$ are disjoint with union $A=\{\max_{k\le n}M_k\ge\lambda\}$. By the submartingale property $\Exp[M_n\given\F_k]\ge M_k$, so $\Exp[M_n\indic_{A_k}]=\Exp[\indic_{A_k}\Exp[M_n\given\F_k]]\ge\Exp[M_k\indic_{A_k}]\ge\lambda\Prob(A_k)$. Summing over $k$: $\Exp[M_n]\ge\Exp[M_n\indic_A]\ge\lambda\Prob(A)$.
(Kolmogorov’s inequality, Theorem 11.9, is the special case $M_k=S_k^2$, which is a non-negative submartingale for mean-zero independent increments.)
Let $M$ be a martingale with $\abs{M_k-M_{k-1}}\le c_k$ for constants $c_k$. Then for $t>0$,
\Prob(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le\exp\Bigl(-\frac{t^2}{2\sum_{k=1}^nc_k^2}\Bigr),
and the same bound holds for $\Prob(M_n-M_0\le-t)$.

Let $D_k=M_k-M_{k-1}$. Given $\F_{k-1}$, $D_k$ has conditional mean $0$ and lies in $[-c_k,c_k]$, an interval of length $2c_k$. Hoeffding’s lemma (Lemma 10.17), applied to the conditional distribution, gives $\Exp[e^{sD_k}\given\F_{k-1}]\le e^{s^2(2c_k)^2/8}=e^{s^2c_k^2/2}$. Iterating the tower property,

\Exp[e^{s(M_n-M_0)}]=\Exp\bigl[e^{s(M_{n-1}-M_0)}\Exp[e^{sD_n}\given\F_{n-1}]\bigr]
\le e^{s^2c_n^2/2}\Exp[e^{s(M_{n-1}-M_0)}]\le\dots\le e^{s^2\sum c_k^2/2}.
By Markov’s inequality, $\Prob(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le e^{-st+s^2\sum c_k^2/2}$; the best $s$ is $t/\sum c_k^2$, giving the bound. The lower tail follows by applying this to $-M$.

Let $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ change by at most $c_k$ when only the $k$th coordinate changes, and let $X_i$ be independent. The Doob martingale $M_k=\Exp[f(X)\given X_1,\dots,X_k]$ has $\abs{M_k-M_{k-1}}\le c_k$ (resampling $X_k$ changes $f$ by at most $c_k$ in conditional expectation), $M_0=\Exp[f(X)]$ and $M_n=f(X)$. Azuma gives McDiarmid’s inequality: $\Prob(f(X)-\Exp f(X)\ge t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\sum c_k^2)}$ (a sharper constant, $e^{-2t^2/\sum c_k^2}$, holds with a more careful argument). Application: the number $D$ of distinct values among $n$ uniform draws from $m$ boxes changes by at most $1$ per draw, so $\Prob(\abs{D-\Exp D}\ge t)\le2e^{-t^2/(2n)}$.

Let $M$ be a martingale, $a<b$, and let $U_n$ be the number of upcrossings of $[a,b]$ by $M_0,\dots,M_n$ (passages from below $a$ to above $b$). Then $(b-a)\Exp[U_n]\le\Exp[(M_n-a)^-]$, where $x^-=\max(-x,0)$.

Define a predictable betting strategy: $H_k=1$ (“hold one unit”) from the first time after $M$ drops below $a$ until the next time it exceeds $b$, and $H_k=0$ otherwise. Formally $H_1=\indic_{\{M_0<a\}}$ and $H_k=\indic_{\{H_{k-1}=1,M_{k-1}\le b\}}+\indic_{\{H_{k-1}=0,M_{k-1}<a\}}$; $H_k$ depends on $M_0,\dots,M_{k-1}$, so it is predictable. Each completed upcrossing earns at least $b-a$ in $(H\cdot M)$. A final incomplete stretch (bought below $a$ and not yet sold above $b$) can lose at most $(M_n-a)^-$. Hence $(H\cdot M)_n\ge(b-a)U_n-(M_n-a)^-$. By Theorem 14.4, $\Exp[(H\cdot M)_n]=0$, and the claim follows.
If $M$ is a martingale with $\sup_n\Exp\abs{M_n}<\infty$, then $M_n$ converges almost surely to a finite limit $M_\infty$. In particular every non-negative martingale converges almost surely.

Let $C=\sup_n\Exp\abs{M_n}$. By the upcrossing inequality, $\Exp[U_n]\le(C+\abs a)/(b-a)$ for all $n$, so the total number of upcrossings $U_\infty=\lim U_n$ has finite expectation, hence is finite almost surely. A real sequence that has only finitely many upcrossings of every rational interval $[a,b]$ cannot oscillate (if $\liminf<\limsup$ there would be rationals $a<b$ between them with infinitely many upcrossings), so $M_n$ converges in $[-\infty,\infty]$ almost surely. By Fatou’s lemma (Chapter 15), $\Exp\abs{M_\infty}\le\liminf\Exp\abs{M_n}\le C<\infty$, so the limit is finite almost surely. For $M\ge0$, $\Exp\abs{M_n}=\Exp[M_n]=\Exp[M_0]$ is constant.

Start the urn with one red and one blue ball. After $n$ draws, let $K$ be the number of red balls added. Any particular sequence with $k$ red draws has probability $\frac{k!\,(n-k)!}{2\cdot3\cdots(n+1)}=\frac{k!(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}$ (the numerators $1,2,\dots,k$ for red and $1,\dots,n-k$ for blue, denominators $2,3,\dots,n+1$), independent of the order. Since there are $\binom nk$ such sequences, $\Prob(K=k)=\binom nk\frac{k!(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}=\frac1{n+1}$: uniform on $\{0,\dots,n\}$. The fraction red is $F_n=(K+1)/(n+2)$, which converges in distribution to $U(0,1)$. Since $F_n$ is a bounded martingale it converges almost surely by Theorem 14.15; the limit therefore has the uniform law. So each run of the urn settles to a random proportion, uniformly distributed, and that proportion is determined by the early draws.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: convergence a.s. need not mean convergence in $L^1$

blocks.x: The martingale $M_n=\prod_{i\le n}Y_i$ with $Y_i$ i.i.d., $\Prob(Y=0)=\Prob(Y=2)=\tfrac12$, has $\Exp[M_n]=1$ for all $n$, but $M_n\to0$ almost surely (the first zero factor kills it). So $\Exp[M_\infty]=0\ne1$. Almost sure convergence of an $L^1$-bounded martingale does not imply convergence of expectations; this requires uniform integrability. This is the same phenomenon as in Example 11.3(ii).

Suppose rewards $g_0,g_1,\dots,g_N$ are revealed over time (adapted), and we may choose a stopping time $\tau\le N$ to collect $g_\tau$. What is the best expected reward, and what is the best stopping rule?

Define $V_N=g_N$ and $V_n=\max\bigl(g_n,\Exp[V_{n+1}\given\F_n]\bigr)$ for $n<N$ (the value of the best strategy from time $n$ on). Then $\sup_{\tau\le N}\Exp[g_\tau]=\Exp[V_0]$, and the supremum is attained by $\tau^*=\min\{n:g_n=V_n\}$ (stop as soon as the reward at least equals the value of continuing).

By construction $V_n\ge g_n$ and $V_n\ge\Exp[V_{n+1}\given\F_n]$, so $V$ is a supermartingale dominating $g$. For any stopping time $\tau\le N$, $V_{\tau\wedge n}$ is a supermartingale (the transform argument of Theorem 14.6 with inequality), so $\Exp[g_\tau]\le\Exp[V_\tau]\le\Exp[V_0]$. For $\tau^*$: before $\tau^*$ we have $V_n>g_n$, so $V_n=\Exp[V_{n+1}\given\F_n]$, which means $V_{\tau^*\wedge n}$ is a martingale and $\Exp[V_{\tau^*}]=\Exp[V_0]$; also $V_{\tau^*}=g_{\tau^*}$ (at time $N$, $V_N=g_N$). Hence $\Exp[g_{\tau^*}]=\Exp[V_0]$.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Rolling a die up to three times

blocks.x: You roll a fair die up to $3$ times and may stop at any roll, taking its value as your reward. Work backwards. With one roll left the value is $V_1=\Exp[X]=3.5$. With two rolls left you stop on the first roll if it exceeds $3.5$: $V_2=\Exp[\max(X,3.5)]=\frac{3\cdot3.5+4+5+6}6=4.25$. With three rolls left you stop on the first roll if it exceeds $4.25$ (i.e. is at least $5$): $V_3=\Exp[\max(X,4.25)]=\frac{4\cdot4.25+5+6}6=\frac{28}6\approx4.667$.

$n$ candidates, all with distinct quality, arrive in uniformly random order. After each interview you see only the relative rank of the candidate among those seen so far, and must immediately accept or reject; a rejected candidate cannot be recalled. To maximise the probability of choosing the overall best candidate, use the rule: reject the first $r-1$ candidates, then accept the first candidate who is the best so far. The success probability is
P_n(r)=\frac{r-1}n\sum_{k=r}^n\frac1{k-1}\qquad(r\ge2),
the optimal $r$ is approximately $n/e$, and the optimal success probability tends to $1/e\approx0.368$ as $n\to\infty$.

Success probability. The rule picks the overall best candidate exactly when, for some position $k\ge r$, the best candidate is at position $k$ and the best of the first $k-1$ candidates is among the first $r-1$ (so that no one between positions $r$ and $k-1$ was the best so far). The best candidate is at position $k$ with probability $1/n$, and independently the best among the first $k-1$ is in the first $r-1$ positions with probability $(r-1)/(k-1)$ (by exchangeability of the relative order). Summing over $k$ gives $P_n(r)$.

Optimality of threshold rules. Stopping at a best-so-far candidate at time $k$ wins with probability $k/n$ (the best of the first $k$ is the overall best). The value $c_k$ of continuing optimally after time $k$ is non-increasing in $k$ (fewer chances remain), while $k/n$ is increasing. So the set of $k$ at which stopping (given a best-so-far) is optimal is $\{k:k/n\ge c_k\}$, an upper interval $\{r,r+1,\dots,n\}$, by Theorem 14.17 applied with state “this candidate is best so far”. The optimal rule is therefore a threshold rule of the form above, and it remains to optimise over $r$.

Asymptotics. Put $x=r/n$. Then $P_n(r)=\frac{r-1}n\sum_{k=r}^n\frac1{k-1}\to x\int_x^1\frac{du}u=-x\ln x$. This is maximised where $\frac d{dx}(-x\ln x)=-\ln x-1=0$, i.e. $x=1/e$, with maximum value $1/e$.

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: the secretary rule and its cousins

blocks.x: “Look at the first $37\%$, then leap at the first one better than everything seen” wins with probability about $37\%$, remarkably independent of $n$. Variants: maximise the expected rank (the answer is a different threshold sequence), allow a probability of recall, or let the number of candidates be unknown. In every variant, work backwards from the last stage: $V_n=\max(\text{stop},\text{continue})$.

Show that for a symmetric simple random walk $S_n^3-3nS_n$ is a martingale and use it with optional stopping to compute $\Exp[\tau]$ and $\Exp[\tau\mid S_\tau=N]$ for the walk started at $0$ and stopped on hitting $\pm N$.
Show that $\Exp[\tau]=N^2$ for the symmetric walk from $0$ stopped on exiting $(-N,N)$.
Use Example 14.10 to find the expected number of tosses to get HHTHH, THT and HTHT.

Two players keep tossing a fair coin; $A$ wins when HH first appears, $B$ wins when HT first appears. Show that $B$ wins with probability $\tfrac12$ (in fact, they alternate on the same sequence). Then for the patterns HH vs. TH show who is more likely to win.
Prove that if $M$ is a martingale and $\varphi$ is convex with $\Exp\abs{\varphi(M_n)}<\infty$ then $\varphi(M_n)$ is a submartingale. (Jensen for conditional expectation.)
A fair die is rolled up to $4$ times with the option to stop. Find the value of the optimal stopping problem and the optimal rule.
In the secretary problem with $n=10$, compute $P_{10}(r)$ for each $r$ and find the best threshold.

(Challenge) Show that the condition $\Exp[\tau]<\infty$ in Theorem 14.7(c) cannot be dropped: give a martingale with bounded increments and an a.s. finite stopping time $\tau$ with $\Exp[\tau]=\infty$ and $\Exp[M_\tau]\ne\Exp[M_0]$.
